name: Annotated dataset-example panel
summary: Dataset snippets arranged into cells by activation level, with two independent quantities painted onto each token: orange shading for how hard the feature fires, and a coloured underline for how much that token's predicted log-likelihood moved when the feature was ablated. It is how the paper shows a feature's causal effect and audits feature-proxy disagreements one case at a time, by inspection and count rather than by measurement.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Two questions push the paper to annotate text rather than plot it. Does a [[feature]] change what the model predicts, and on which tokens? And when a feature disagrees with an independent [[computational-proxy]] for the same hypothesis, which is wrong? Both are claims about alignment: that a measured quantity lands on exactly the tokens a reader would have pointed to. No axis can hold "this token is Arabic script", so the text becomes the substrate and the measurements are drawn onto it.

A bar of mean logit change would say the [[arabic-script-feature]] helps Arabic predictions and lose the fact that the only tokens it hurts are punctuation shared with other scripts, the detail that makes the interpretation specific. For the [[dna-feature]] the paper quotes a Pearson correlation of $0.8$ between activations and the binarized proxy; that says disagreement exists, not whose fault it is. The grid exists so the authors can open each disagreement and assign blame.

### How to read it, step by step

No y-axis; the layout encodes conditions. Columns are bands of the feature's firing range — in fig-11 two [[activation-interval]]s, the top band and a middle band at about half that activation; in fig-21 four sampled levels including exactly-off, each tied by a dotted line to a histogram underneath. Two rows, where present, carry a second variable: the proxy's yes/no verdict after [[proxy-binarization]].

A cell holds five or six snippets, each a nine-token window: a bold selected token whose activation put the example in that cell, four tokens of context either side, drawn from a 100-million-token subset ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]).

The unit to read is a token, carrying two encodings that need not agree. Orange background is [[feature-activation]], the ReLU output of one [[sparse-autoencoder]] hidden unit, darker for stronger. The underline is a separate experiment: the context is run again with this feature's activation times its [[feature-direction]] subtracted from the MLP activations throughout ([[feature-ablation]]), and reports how far that token's predicted log-likelihood moved. Purple or blue means it fell, so the feature had been helping predict that token; orange-red means it rose, so the feature had been hurting; flat grey means nothing moved; thickness and saturation give size. The scale is unlabelled, so compare underlines within a figure only ([[ablation-effect-visualization]]).

One ablation produces a whole row of underlines, so the informative cases are mismatches: a heavily shaded token with a flat underline is one the feature fires on without being used for. Start at the legend inset, then the agreeing cells, then the off-diagonal ones. In fig-11 Arabic glyphs render on a lower line while half-character byte tokens sit above as escape codes, each shaded and underlined on its own ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]).

### What a bad result would look like

For the ablation panel: purple under Latin tokens as often as Arabic ones; or every underline flat grey, meaning the direction describes the data and the MLP does not use it; or half-activation examples underlined as heavily as full-activation ones, breaking the roughly linear story the [[logit-weight]] approximation assumes ([[large-activations-dominate]]).

For the audit grid: the proxy-fires-feature-off cell filled with plain nucleotide runs the feature missed ([[activation-sensitivity]]), and the feature-fires-proxy-silent row filled with ordinary English ([[activation-specificity]]). Then blame falls on the feature, and the correlation was flattering it.

Count honestly either way: ten and forty-eight hand-read examples, adjudicated by the authors, on features the paper says were chosen for being tractable ([[cherry-picked-case-studies]]). "One genuine error out of six" tallies a display, not a population, and blaming the other twenty-two disagreements on [[proxy-limitations]] is a judgement checkable only on the examples shown.

### Where it comes back

fig-11 (3.1.3) is the ablation form: one feature, no proxy, columns as activation bands. fig-21 (3.2.1) is the audit form: random rather than top examples ([[top-dataset-examples]]), a proxy verdict on the rows, no underlines, a histogram welded underneath. What changes is what the cells condition on and whether underlines are drawn at all. The same annotated snippet is the atom of the [[feature-exploration-interface]]; fig-12 answers the same causal question by generation instead ([[pinned-feature-sampling]]).
